summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to order the materials for a fabrication job as a team leader: work out quantities from the drawings with cutting lists and nesting, describe every item fully, compare suppliers on value, time the orders to the job programme, raise and get approval for purchase orders within the budget, receive and check deliveries for coded work, store materials correctly, keep stock under control and review the ordering after the job.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). A fabrication job can only start on time, within budget and to the drawing if the right materials, in the right amounts, arrive at the right time with the right paperwork. As team leader you work out what is needed, order it properly, check what arrives, and learn from each job to order better next time.

At Level 2 you helped to list and receive materials. At Level 3 you take charge of the whole cycle, including the calculations, the comparison of suppliers and imports, the timing against the job programme, the budget, the rules on approval and ethics, and the extra checks and records that coded work needs.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and charge hands, leading hands and storekeepers in Jamaican fabrication shops and maintenance departments.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Make a cutting list from checked drawings, plan cuts from stock lengths, nest plate parts, add a waste allowance, and list bought items and consumables.
Work out masses, areas, electrodes and wire, paint, mesh sheets, costs, discounts and landed costs.
Write order lines that give the size, section, grade, standard, length, quantity, finish and certificates, so the supplier cannot get it wrong.
Get written quotations from approved suppliers and compare price, delivery, lead time, terms and quality, not just price.
Work back from the job programme and the lead times, order long-lead items first, and allow for imports and the hurricane season.
Check the need, the stock and the budget; raise the requisition and purchase order; get approval; check the order confirmation; follow it up.
Check deliveries against the order and certificates, record and deal with problems, store materials correctly, and match invoices before payment.
Keep stock records, set reorder levels, deal with dead stock, keep the paperwork that makes materials traceable, and review each job's ordering.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on quantities and cutting lists, masses, describing materials, consumables and gases, suppliers, lead times, stock control, approval, order documents, costing and GCT, ethics, receiving and problems, paperwork, storage, substitutes, imports and reviewing orders.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and quick sums, such as cutting list, 7850, order confirmation, dead stock, heat number, request for quotation, approved supplier list) and essays on quantities, suppliers, describing materials, lead times, stock control, receiving, costing, ethics, substitutes and review.

**Practical tasks**: producing a cutting list, a cutting plan and a priced, approved purchase order for a job; and receiving a delivery for a coded job with planted problems, dealing with them, storing it and updating the stock records.

blocks.note: Show your working in every calculation, and state your answer with its unit (m, kg, sheets, packets, J$). In the practicals, the assessor checks the method as well as the answer.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: From drawings to a materials list

blocks.p: Start from **checked, approved drawings**, never from last month's order, a supplier's special offer or a guess. Order only once the drawings and the cutting list are checked; ordering before the client has agreed the job, or on the morning work starts, causes waste or delay.
A **cutting list** gives every piece to be cut for the job: its mark, section, size, length and number off. Group the pieces by section so each section can be planned and ordered on its own.

Steel is sold in standard lengths, often 6 m (many Jamaican stockists sell 20 ft, about 6.1 m: check the real length). The total length divided by the stock length only gives the **least possible** number; the real number comes from a **cutting plan** that fits whole pieces into each length, allowing for each saw cut (the **kerf**, often about 2–3 mm).

head: Cutting plan for U1 and R1 from 6 m lengths
Pieces
Used
Offcut
rows: About 1.3 m: keep it if it is useful

blocks.p: The total is 15.9 m, and 15.9 ÷ 6 = 2.65, so at least 3 lengths are needed; the plan shows 3 lengths really do work. Always check the plan: sometimes the total says one number but the pieces will not fit, and one more length is needed.

Draw plate parts (base plates, gussets, treads) on a sketch of the full sheet, which is called **nesting**, to find the fewest sheets with the least waste. Common sheets are 1220 × 2440 mm (4 × 8 ft), 1500 × 3000 mm and 1500 × 6000 mm. The area of the parts alone can mislead: long or awkward parts may not fit even when their total area is less than the sheet's.

blocks.h: Waste allowance and the rest of the list

ul: Add a **waste allowance** for saw cuts, offcuts that cannot be used and mistakes: often about 5–10%, or what the shop's records show for that kind of job.
Add the **bought items**: hinges, bolts and nuts, anchors, locks, castors, mesh.
Add the **consumables**: electrodes or wire, shielding gas, cutting and grinding discs, cutting gas.
Add the **finishing materials**: primer and paint, galvanising (if bought in), thinners.
Check the **store** before ordering: usable offcuts and stock of the right size and grade can be used, and only the balance ordered. On coded work, offcuts must be traceable to their certificates.

blocks.p: Steel weighs about **7 850 kg per cubic metre** (7.85 g per cm³). You need the mass to price steel sold by weight, to plan transport and unloading, and to choose lifting equipment.

ul: **Plate:** mass = length (m) × width (m) × thickness (m) × 7 850. A 1220 × 2440 × 8 mm sheet: 1.22 × 2.44 × 0.008 × 7 850 = about 187 kg.
**Sections:** mass = length × mass per metre from the supplier's or a steel table. 18 lengths of 6 m angle at 2.4 kg/m: 18 × 6 × 2.4 = about 259 kg.
**Area of a sheet:** length × width: a 1500 × 3000 mm sheet is 1.5 × 3.0 = 4.5 m².
**Flat bar:** 60 × 10 mm flat bar is 0.06 × 0.01 × 7 850 = 4.71 kg/m, so a 3.2 m length weighs 3.2 × 4.71 = 15.1 kg.

flow: Work out the weld metal: for a fillet, cross-section ≈ leg × leg ÷ 2; × total length; × 7.85 g per cm³
Divide by the deposit efficiency to get the filler to buy (for example about 55–65% for stick electrodes, after stubs, slag and spatter; about 80–90% for flux-cored wire; more for solid wire)
Round **up** to whole packets or spools, and add a little for test pieces and tacks
Order the **exact classification and size** on the WPS: the procedure was proved with that filler

ul: **Paint:** litres = area × number of coats ÷ coverage (m² per litre per coat), plus waste; then round up to whole tins. Check the paint's shelf life before buying a lot.
**Mesh, sheeting and similar:** sheets = area needed × (1 + waste allowance) ÷ area of one sheet, rounded up.
**Discs:** order the right type (cutting or grinding), the right diameter and bore, and a maximum speed (rpm) **at least** the grinder's speed: a disc rated below the grinder's speed can burst.
**Gases:** estimate from flow rate × arc time, or from past use per job; order full cylinders to swap for empties.
Item cost = unit price × quantity: 4.5 m of beam at J$11 200 per metre = J$50 400; 8 packets at J$4 900 = J$39 200.
Discount = price × discount rate: 3% of J$65 000 = J$1 950.
Add delivery charges, and GCT at the **current rate** where it applies. Check that each quotation's GCT is charged at the current rate, and whether prices include it, before comparing.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, or have another team member check it. A slip of one decimal place on a steel order costs far more than the time it takes to check.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: If an order line is incomplete, the supplier has to guess, and the wrong item may arrive: the job stops, time is wasted, and the work may not meet the design. Each line must describe the item so fully that only one product fits it.

head: Item
What the order line must give
Example
rows: Thickness, sheet size, grade or standard, number of sheets, certificates if needed
2 sheets, 8 mm, 1220 × 2440 mm, grade as specified, with mill certificates
50 × 6 mm flat bar, mild steel, 6 m lengths, qty 4
Leg sizes × thickness (or depth × flange), grade, length, quantity
50 × 50 × 5 mm equal angle, grade as specified, 6 m, qty 12
Designation (for example W8 × 18 or 203 × 133 UB 25), grade, length, quantity, certificates
W8 × 18 beam, grade as drawing, 6 m, qty 8, mill certificates
Shape (SHS, RHS, CHS), outside sizes, wall thickness, grade, length, quantity
50 × 50 × 3.0 mm SHS, grade as specified, 6 m, qty 10
Nominal size and outside diameter, wall thickness or **schedule**, grade, black or galvanised, ends, length, quantity
50 NB (60.3 mm OD) Sch 40, black, grade as specified, plain ends, 6 m, qty 10
Classification, diameter, packet size, number of packets, batch numbers shown
E7018, 3.2 mm, 5 kg packets, qty 6, batch numbers on packets
Classification, diameter, spool size and type, quantity
The exact gas or mixture, cylinder size, full-for-empty exchange or new rental
Argon 80% / CO2 20%, large cylinder, 2 full for 2 empty

ul: Structural steel must be ordered by **grade** (for example ASTM A36 plate or A992 beams, or the grade the drawing names), because the design depends on its strength and the WPS on its weldability.

For coded or structural work, ask for **mill certificates** (material test certificates). They give the **heat number** (the number of one melt of steel, stamped or painted on the steel), the chemistry and the test results, and prove the steel meets its grade.
Pipe of the same nominal size comes in different wall thicknesses (schedules) and grades. Two pipes that look the same on the outside can have very different strength.

blocks.p: Much steel sold in Jamaica is made to American standards, in inches and feet, while drawings are often metric. 1 in = 25.4 mm, so ¼ in plate is 6.35 mm and ⅜ in is 9.5 mm; 1 ft = 304.8 mm, so a 20 ft length is about 6.1 m. Where the drawing's size and the stock size differ, agree the equivalent with the person responsible for the design; do not assume.

Most organisations keep an **approved supplier list**: suppliers that have been checked (quality, certificates, reliability, prices, terms) and may be used. A new supplier is vetted and added to the list before an order is placed with it.

flow: Write one **request for quotation (RFQ)** with full descriptions, quantities, certificates needed, delivery address and the date needed
Send the same RFQ to several approved suppliers (often at least three for a large order)
Put the replies side by side on a comparison sheet
Check each one quotes exactly what was asked: grade, size, certificates
Compare total cost, lead time, delivery, terms, validity and past performance
Recommend a supplier with reasons, and get approval

head: Supplier
Quotation
Delivery
Lead time
Notes
rows: Not on the approved list; no certificates offered

blocks.p: Before GCT, A totals J$420 000 and B J$416 000. C looks cheapest, but it is not approved and offers no certificates, so it cannot be used for certified steel. B is J$4 000 cheaper than A, but takes 10 days: if the job needs the steel in a week, A is the better value. **The lowest price is not always the best choice**: late delivery, the wrong grade, missing certificates or hidden charges can cost far more than the saving.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The price includes carriage to your site
The price is at the supplier's yard: you collect, or pay extra for transport
The full invoice amount is due within 30 days of the invoice date
Payment is made when the goods arrive
After 30 days the supplier may change the price: ask them to confirm or re-quote
A reduction if the invoice is paid within a set time

blocks.p: Special steels, stainless pipe and fittings are often imported. To compare an overseas price fairly with a local one, work out the **landed cost**: everything paid to get the goods to your site.

head: Part of the landed cost
Example
rows: Total in US$, at the job's exchange rate of J$156 to US$1
Customs duty (as worked out by the customs broker)
Clearing, port and local delivery charges

blocks.note: Goods are cleared through the Jamaica Customs Agency, usually by a licensed **customs broker**, who can confirm the duty and charges before you compare. GCT is also charged on imports at the current rate. Allow time for shipping and clearance in the lead time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Keep a simple record for each supplier: deliveries on time, complete and correct; how quickly problems were fixed; quality of certificates. Use it when choosing suppliers and when reviewing the approved list.

sections.title: Timing the orders and controlling stock

flow: Take the job programme: when cutting, fabrication, welding, painting and installation start
For each material, find the date it is needed on site
Find each lead time from the supplier, including freight and customs for imports
Work back: latest order date = date needed − lead time − safety time
Order long-lead items (imports, special grades) first, on the day the job is confirmed
Time other deliveries to arrive just before they are needed, so the yard is not crowded and paint does not pass its shelf life
Put order and delivery dates on a chart; follow up with suppliers; report likely delays early

blocks.p: If an item cannot arrive in time (for example imported galvanised pipe that takes 6 weeks for a job that starts in 4), tell the supervisor **now**, and agree a new date or another source. Starting with the wrong material, or saying nothing, makes it worse.

blocks.note: The Atlantic hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November. Shipping, ports and roads are more likely to be delayed then, and demand for steel and building materials can rise after a storm. Order key materials earlier and keep a little more safety time in those months.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Keep a **bin card** or a spreadsheet line for every stock item: stock in, stock out (against a job), and the balance.
Issue **first in, first out (FIFO)**: older packets in front, so nothing passes its shelf life.
Do regular **stocktakes** and investigate differences between the count and the records.
Keep full and empty gas cylinders in separate, marked places, and track every rented cylinder by its number: rent is charged until each one is returned.

blocks.p: **Reorder level = usage during the lead time + safety stock.** When the balance falls to the reorder level, order. The safety stock is there for late deliveries or a busy week.

head: Example: grinding discs
Working
rows: Maximum stock set by the manager
Stock when the order arrives ≈ 65 − 50 = 15, so order 120 − 15 = 105 discs

ul: **Too little:** jobs stop, rush orders cost more.
**Too much:** money is tied up, shelves fill, and electrodes, paint and wire can spoil before use.
**Dead stock** is stock that has not moved for a long time and is unlikely to be used. Report it so the manager can decide to return, sell, use (where a WPS allows) or scrap it.
A bulk discount (for example 10% for a year's wire) is worth it only after thinking about storage space, cash, shelf life and real need.

sections.title: Requisitions, approval and the purchase order

flow: A welder or supervisor raises a **purchase requisition**: what is needed, how much, for which job, by when
The team leader checks the need, the stock in the store and the budget
The requisition is approved by someone with the authority for that amount
A **purchase order (PO)** is raised to the chosen supplier, with its own PO number
The supplier sends an **order confirmation** (acknowledgement); check it line by line against the PO
Follow up (expedite) before the delivery date, and record any change

ul: The **PO number** (used to match the delivery note, goods received note and invoice), date, and job number
The supplier's name and address, and the delivery address and date
Full descriptions, quantities, units and unit prices of every item
Delivery charges, discounts, GCT at the current rate, and the total
Certificates and documents required
Payment terms, and the signature of the person approving it

blocks.note: If the order confirmation shows a different item, size or date from your order (for example 3.2 mm electrodes when you ordered 2.5 mm), have it corrected **at once**, before the goods are sent.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Each person may approve orders only up to their **authority limit**. Above it, the order goes to the person with that authority.
Never **split** an order into smaller ones to get each under your limit: it hides the true spend and breaks the rules.

Compare the order total with the job's materials budget before ordering. If it is over, look for savings that keep the quality (better nesting, usable offcuts, a cheaper approved supplier, combined deliveries). If it is still over, tell the supervisor before ordering: only they can agree to spend more.

blocks.p: When a supplier cannot provide the grade or section on the drawing, first try to get the specified item, from another approved supplier if need be. Never accept a different grade or section yourself, even a 'stronger' one or one at the same price: it may weld differently, need a different filler or WPS, not fit the other parts, or change the design. Get the details and take them to the engineer or the person responsible for the design for **written approval**. If it is approved, update the order, the drawing or change note, the cutting list and the WPS if needed, and tell the team.

head: Rule
Why it matters
rows: Refuse gifts, money or favours from suppliers, and tell your supervisor about any offer
They can bias the choice; accepting them can be corruption
Declare any family or business link with a supplier, and stand back from decisions about it
A conflict of interest, even an honest one, makes the choice look unfair
Choose suppliers fairly on value, and keep the quotations and the reasons
The choice can be shown to be honest
Telling one supplier another's price is unfair and breaks trust
Use materials only for the Centre's or the company's jobs
Keep orders written, numbered and recorded
Deliveries, invoices and payments can be checked

flow: Prepare a clear, safe unloading area, with lifting equipment and trained people ready
Before signing anything, check the delivery note against the purchase order
Count lengths, sheets, packets and spools; measure sizes and thicknesses with a tape and vernier
Check the condition: bends, deep pitting, rust on wire, damaged or wet packets
For coded work, check the heat numbers on the steel against the mill certificates, and that the certificates show the grade ordered
Write every shortage, wrong item, damage or missing certificate on the delivery note **before** signing
Quarantine and label failed items; report them; raise a discrepancy report and, for returns, a returns note quoting the PO and delivery note numbers
Fill in a **goods received note (GRN)** and book the accepted items into the stock records against the job

blocks.note: Do not sign 'received in good order' because the driver is in a hurry. A signature on a clean delivery note tells the supplier everything was right, and makes a later claim much harder.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Problem
What to do
rows: Note the shortfall on the delivery note; sign only for what arrived; chase the balance
Wrong size or grade (for example 6 mm plate on an 8 mm order)
Note it; refuse it or quarantine it; report it; do not use it 'for small parts'
Heat number not on any certificate
Quarantine and label it until the correct certificate arrives
Record and photograph; keep apart; claim from the supplier
Tell the supervisor, re-plan the work, record it

ul: Steel on racks off the ground, sorted by section, labelled with the job and heat number for coded work.
**Certified steel for a coded job kept apart** from general stock and labelled, so it cannot be mixed up with, or used as, other steel.
Low-hydrogen electrodes from opened packets in a **holding oven**, as the maker says; other consumables in a dry store.
Gas cylinders upright and chained, in the right store, with full and empty apart.
Heavy items at waist height; walkways clear.

blocks.p: Before an invoice is paid, the office matches three documents: the **purchase order** (what was ordered and at what price), the **goods received note** (what actually arrived and was accepted), and the **invoice** (what the supplier is charging). Any difference, such as a charge for items that never came, a different price or the wrong GCT, is queried with the supplier before payment.

ul: Requisitions, quotations and the comparison sheet with the reasons for the choice
Purchase orders, order confirmations and any changes
Delivery notes, GRNs, discrepancy reports and returns notes
Mill certificates and consumable certificates, kept with the job records so the steel can be shown to meet the specification
The supplier, batch and date of every lot of electrodes and wire, so a faulty batch can be traced and recalled
Invoices and the three-way match

blocks.h: Reviewing the ordering after the job

flow: List what was ordered, used, left over and scrapped, for steel, consumables and paint
Work out the waste as a percentage for each: for example 15% of the steel left over
Find the reasons: poor nesting, cutting mistakes, design changes, damaged deliveries, over-ordering
Review the suppliers: on time, complete, correct, quick to fix problems
Compare the actual cost with the budget
Agree actions (better nesting, a different waste allowance, earlier orders, another supplier) and record them
Label useful offcuts and book them into stock for the next job

blocks.note: Leftover steel is not 'normal' or someone else's fault. Finding out why is how the next estimate gets better.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can make a cutting list from checked drawings and plan cuts from stock lengths, allowing for the kerf.
I can nest plate parts on a sheet and explain why area alone can mislead.
I can add a sensible waste allowance and list bought items, consumables and finishing materials.
I can work out the mass of plate and sections, and the electrodes, wire, paint and sheets needed.
I can write an order line that describes plate, sections, pipe, electrodes, wire and gas fully.
I can explain grades, mill certificates and heat numbers, and convert inch sizes to millimetres.
I can send RFQs to approved suppliers and compare quotations on value, not just price.
I can work out the landed cost of an imported item.
I can time orders from the job programme and lead times, including imports and the hurricane season.
I can set a reorder level and an order quantity, and deal with dead stock.
I can raise a requisition and a purchase order, and check an order confirmation.
I can work within my authority limit and the budget, and deal with substitutes properly.
I can follow the ethics rules on gifts, conflicts of interest and confidentiality.
I can receive and check a delivery, record problems before signing, and quarantine failed items.
I can store steel, consumables and cylinders correctly.
I can explain three-way matching.
I can review the ordering after a job and improve the next one.

terms: Approved supplier list
The register of suppliers checked and allowed to be used
Bin card
A stock record of items in, out and the balance
Cutting list
The list of every piece to cut, with section, length and number off
Cutting plan
How the pieces will be cut from each stock length
Customs duty
The government charge on goods brought into Jamaica

Stock unused for a long time and unlikely to be used
Delivery note
The supplier's list of what was sent, signed on receipt
Ex-works
A price at the supplier's yard, without delivery
FIFO
First in, first out: oldest stock used first
Goods received note (GRN)
The record of what was received and accepted
Heat number

Kerf

Landed cost

The steelmaker's certificate of grade, chemistry and tests
Nesting
Arranging plate parts on a sheet to use the fewest sheets

The supplier's acceptance of an order, with items, prices and date

Purchase requisition

Usage during the lead time plus safety stock

A request to several suppliers to price the same items

Three-way matching
Checking the order, goods received and invoice agree

c1.title: A canteen staircase in Chapelton
c1.text: Tracy-Ann is the team leader for a steel staircase at a school canteen in Chapelton, Clarendon. The cutting list has 2 stringers of 150 × 75 mm channel, each 3.6 m long, and 3 landing beams of the same channel, each 1.6 m long. The channel comes in 6 m lengths. The 9 treads are each 1100 × 280 mm, to be cut from 1220 × 2440 mm chequer plate. The store has one sound 2.1 m offcut of the same channel and grade.

c2.title: Imported fittings for a hotel pool plant in Discovery Bay
c2.text: Romaine is ordering for stainless pipework at a hotel's pool plant in Discovery Bay, St Ann. An overseas supplier quotes US$2 400 for the special flanged fittings, plus US$350 freight and insurance; the job uses J$157 to US$1. Customs duty is estimated at J$62 000 and clearing and port charges at J$28 000. A local agent can supply the same fittings for J$540 000 delivered, in 3 weeks. The import takes about 6 weeks, including shipping and clearance. Fabrication on site starts in 5 weeks. GCT applies the same way to both, so it is left out of the comparison.

c3.title: The consumables store at a shop in Christiana
c3.text: Odane runs the consumables store at a fabrication shop in Christiana, Manchester. The shop uses about 6 spools of 1.2 mm flux-cored wire a week; the supplier takes 3 weeks to deliver, the manager wants 4 spools kept as safety stock, and stock must never go above 30 spools. On a top shelf are 9 boxes of an electrode type the shop stopped using two years ago. The gas supplier's statement shows 5 rented oxygen cylinders on site, but Odane can find only 3.

c4.title: Roof beams for a church in Brown's Town
c4.text: Kerry-Ann checks a delivery of steel for a church roof in Brown's Town, St Ann. The purchase order was for 8 lengths of W8 × 18 beam, grade A992, with mill certificates. Eight lengths arrive, but the heat number painted on two of them is not on any of the certificates. The driver also hands her a note: the supplier has no 6 mm A36 plate for the base plates, and offers 6 mm plate of a higher-strength grade at the same price. The driver is in a hurry and asks her to sign.

c5.title: Quotations for a walkway in Port Antonio
c5.text: Jason is a newly appointed team leader at a fabrication shop in Port Antonio, Portland. He has three written quotations for hollow section for a hotel walkway. One supplier on the approved list is part-owned by his cousin. A sales rep from another supplier phones to ask what prices the others quoted, 'so we can beat them'. The lowest quotation is dated 45 days ago and says 'prices valid for 30 days'.

questions.q: Without using the store's offcut, what is the fewest 6 m lengths of channel that will give all the pieces?
o: 2 lengths
3 lengths
4 lengths
5 lengths
questions.why: The pieces total 12 m, but two 6 m lengths cannot hold them: a 3.6 m and a 1.6 m use 5.2 m of each length, and the third 1.6 m beam needs a third length. Plan whole pieces into each length; do not just divide the total.

questions.q: How does the 2.1 m offcut in the store change the order?
o: It cannot help, as offcuts may never be used on a new job
Order 3 lengths anyway and send the offcut for scrap
Cut the stringers a little shorter so the offcut can be used
The third beam can be cut from it, so 2 lengths are enough
questions.why: The offcut is the same section and grade and sound, so the 1.6 m beam can come from it and only 2 lengths need buying. Checking stock before ordering is part of the job. Changing the drawing's sizes to use up steel is never acceptable.

questions.q: How many sheets of chequer plate are needed for the 9 treads?
o: 2 sheets
1 sheet
3 sheets
9 sheets
questions.why: The treads total 9 × 1.1 × 0.28 = 2.77 m², less than the area of one 1.22 × 2.44 m sheet, but only 8 can be nested on a sheet: a 1100 mm tread fits only twice along 2440 mm and four times across 1220 mm. Nesting, not area alone, decides the number of sheets.

questions.q: What is the landed cost of the imported fittings, before GCT?
questions.why: (US$2 400 + US$350) × 157 = J$431 750, plus J$62 000 duty and J$28 000 clearing = J$521 750. J$431 750 leaves out duty and clearing, J$466 800 leaves out freight, and J$376 800 is the bare price.

questions.q: Which supplier should Romaine recommend?
o: The overseas supplier, as it is J$18 250 cheaper
The overseas supplier, and start the job a week late
The local agent, as it arrives in time for the job
Either one, as their prices are within 5% of each other
questions.why: The import is about J$18 250 cheaper, but it would arrive a week after work must start, and a week's delay on a hotel job costs far more than that. The lowest price is not best value when it misses the programme.

questions.q: Before comparing, Romaine wants the duty and clearing figures confirmed. Who is best placed to do this?
o: A licensed customs broker
The overseas supplier's sales office
The local agent who quoted against it
The hotel's purchasing clerk
questions.why: A customs broker clears goods through the Jamaica Customs Agency every day and can work out the duty and charges for these items. The overseas supplier does not know Jamaican charges, and the competing agent is not independent.

questions.q: What should the reorder level for the wire be?
o: 18 spools
13 spools
10 spools
22 spools
questions.why: Reorder level = usage during the lead time + safety stock = 6 × 3 + 4 = 22 spools. When the balance falls to 22, the order goes in, so the 4 safety spools are still there when the delivery arrives.

questions.q: How many spools should Odane order each time the stock reaches the reorder level?
o: 8 spools
26 spools
30 spools
18 spools
questions.why: During the 3-week wait, 18 spools are used, so about 22 − 18 = 4 are left when the order arrives. To bring stock up to the 30-spool maximum, order 30 − 4 = 26. Ordering 30 − 22 = 8 forgets the spools used while waiting.

questions.q: What should be done about the 9 boxes of unused electrodes?
o: Report them as dead stock for the manager to decide
Keep them, as electrodes never lose their value
Issue them on the next job in place of the WPS type
Throw them out quietly to free up the shelf space
questions.why: Dead stock ties up money and space and may have deteriorated. It is reported so the manager can decide whether to return, sell, use (where a WPS allows) or scrap it, and the stock records are corrected.

questions.q: Which record should show where the two missing cylinders went?
o: The gas supplier's monthly invoice total
The bin card for the flux-cored wire
The cylinder issue log, by cylinder number
The purchase order for the last gas delivery
questions.why: Each rented cylinder has its own number. An issue log that records which cylinder went to which job or site, and when it came back, shows where it is; without it the shop keeps paying rent on cylinders it cannot find.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do with the two beams whose heat numbers are not on the certificates?
o: Use them, since they look the same as the other six beams
Keep them apart, labelled, until certificates come
Use them for the parts of the roof that carry the least load
Accept them, and ask for certificates at the end of the job
questions.why: Without a certificate that matches its heat number, a beam cannot be shown to be the grade ordered. It is kept apart and labelled, the problem is written on the delivery note and reported, and it is used only when the correct certificate arrives.

questions.q: Why should Kerry-Ann not simply accept the higher-strength plate?
o: Higher-strength plate always costs more to cut and drill
Higher-strength plate cannot be welded with any electrode
It would be heavier than the A36 plate it would replace
It may weld differently, and the design used A36
questions.why: A different grade may need a different electrode, preheat or WPS, and the engineer designed the base plates for the specified steel. Only the engineer can approve the change, in writing; then the order, drawing and records are updated.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann write on the delivery note before she signs?
o: Nothing, as the count of eight beams is correct and complete
Received in good order, subject to checking later on
The driver's name and the time he left the site
Two beams' heat numbers are not on the certificates
questions.why: Problems must be written on the delivery note before it is signed, so the supplier cannot later say the goods were accepted as correct. 'Subject to checking' records nothing specific.

questions.q: What should Jason do about his cousin's company?
o: Choose his cousin's company, as he knows it is honest
Declare the link and stand back from that choice
Leave his cousin's company out of every order
Say nothing, since the company is on the approved list
questions.why: A family link is a conflict of interest, even if Jason would be fair. He declares it to his supervisor and lets someone else judge the quotations, so the choice is fair and is seen to be fair.

questions.q: How should Jason answer the sales rep who asks for the other prices?
o: Give the prices, so the shop gets a cheaper deal
Give the lowest price only, to start a bidding war
Decline: other suppliers' prices are confidential
Give the prices, but only for the hollow section
questions.why: Suppliers quote in confidence. Passing one supplier's prices to another is unfair, breaks trust, and goes against fair purchasing rules. If prices are to be re-quoted, every supplier is asked in the same way.

questions.q: What should Jason do about the lowest quotation, which is now 45 days old?
o: Ask the supplier to confirm the price or re-quote
Order at the old price, as the supplier must honour it
Add 10% to it and compare it with the others
Ignore it and choose the next lowest quotation
questions.why: The quotation was valid for 30 days, so the supplier is free to change the price. Jason asks for written confirmation or a new quotation before comparing or ordering; guessing a figure is not a fair comparison.

questions.q: A frame has 55 m² of surface to paint. The primer covers about 10 m² per litre per coat; it needs 2 coats, plus 10% for waste. How many 4-litre tins should be ordered?
o: 3 tins
4 tins
2 tins
6 tins
questions.why: 55 × 2 ÷ 10 = 11 litres; with 10% waste, 12.1 litres; 12.1 ÷ 4 = 3.03, so 4 tins. 3 tins forgets the waste, and 2 tins forgets the second coat.

questions.q: A quotation gives a price 'ex-works'. What must you remember when comparing it with delivered prices?
o: Add the cost of collecting it or of transport
Take off GCT, since ex-works prices already include it
It is a fixed price that cannot change for a year
It includes delivery anywhere in Jamaica
questions.why: Ex-works means the price is at the supplier's yard: you collect, or pay for transport. Add that cost before comparing it with quotations that are delivered to site.

questions.q: A supplier's terms say 'net 30 days'. What does this mean?
o: A 30% discount applies if the invoice is paid at once
Delivery will take 30 days from the order date
The full amount is due within 30 days of the invoice
The prices are fixed for 30 days and then rise
questions.why: Net 30 means the whole invoice is to be paid within 30 days of its date. Knowing the terms helps the office plan payments and compare suppliers fairly.

questions.q: For a water-line job, which purchase order entry gives the supplier everything needed for the pipe?
o: 10 lengths of 2 in pipe, the usual kind, as soon as you can
10 × 6 m of 50 mm black steel pipe, plain ends, any grade
10 lengths of Sch 40 pipe, galvanised or black, any size
10 × 6 m, 50 NB Sch 40, black, specified grade, plain ends
questions.why: Pipe of one nominal size comes in different wall thicknesses (schedules), grades and finishes, so the entry must give the size, schedule, grade, finish, ends, length and quantity. Leave any of them out and the supplier has to guess.
